It begins with O double bonding down and right to C, which bonds down and left to O, which bonds down to H. C also bonds right to O-. To the right of this is the ATP molecule, where Rib (in a box) bonds right to adenine (in a box) and down to P (in a circle), which bonds down to P (in a circle_, which bonds down to O, which bonds down to P. The fourth point binds down and right, then down and left, the down and right, the down and left, then down and right, where O double bonds to it. It then goes down and left to bond with NH, which bonds down to Lys. Below these three images are three light blue waves. The left wave, located under the ATP and biotinyl-lysine molecules is entitled Catalytic site 1. The middle wave, in bold, states, Pyruvate carboxylase, and the right wave, located under and arrow is entitled Catalytic site 2. To the right of the biotinyl-lysine molecule is a black arrow pointing to the carboxyphosphate molecule in brackets, and indicates this as step 1: Bicarbonate is activated by ATP, forming carboxyphosphate. This arrow has another small arrow darting down to ADP. The carboxyphosphate molecule begins with O double bonding down and right to C, which bonds down and left to O, which bonds down to H (all in red). A red arrow goes from the bond line where O bonds down to H up to the bonds line where C bonds down and left to O. C also bonds right to O, where a red arrow goes from this bond line to O. O bonds right to P, which bonds down to O-, right to O-, and double bonds up to O. A black arrow points right from this to an untitled molecule. This arrow has another arrow dartin down to Pi. Above this arrow is step 2: Carboxyphophate breaks down to CO2. The image this arrow points to is exactly like the biotinl-lysine molecule already described, but above HN are two red dots with an arrow going up then down left to C, which double bonds up to O and double bonds down to O. A red arrow goes from the double bond line from C down and right to O to that O. Below this is a black arrow pointing to the carboxybiotinyl-enzyme. This also has an arrow darting left to H+. This is indicated as step 3: CO2 reacts with biotin to form carboxybiotin. The carboxybiotinyl-enzyme looks exactly like the biotinyl-lysine molecule, except HN bonds left to C, which double bonds up and left to O and binds down and left to O- (all in red). From this is another arrow pointing to another image. This indicates step 4: Biotin transports the CO2 from one active site to the other. This image starts with O double bonding down to the second point of a pentagon. It also has a red arrow pointing from this bond back to O. The first point of the pentagon is HN, and the third point is N, which bonds right to C (pink), which double bonds up and right to O and bonds down and right to O-. A red arrow goes from the bond between N and C to the bond above N on the pentagon. An arrow also goes from the O- to its bond line. The bottom of this pentagon meets the top of a pentagon just below (share this side). In this pentagon, beginning with the left point and going clockwise, S is at the fifth point. The first point binds down and left, then down and right, the down and left, then down and right, then down and left, where O double bonds to it. It then goes down and right to bond with NH, which bonds down to Lys. To the left of this is a black arrow pointing to another molecule. This line has pyruvate joining it. This indicates is it step 5: Biotin is decarboxylated. Pyruvate is converted to its enolate form. The next molecule is exactly like the one just described, but it does not have the pink C double bonding to O and bonding to O and the O at the top is O-. There is a red arrow pointing from that O- down and around to its bond line. On the second side of the pentagon is a double bond side. A red arrow points from this to H, which bonds up to CH2, which bonds up to C. A red arrow goes from the first bond line to the second bond line. C double bonds right to O, where a red arrow points from that bond line to O. C also bonds up to C, which bonds up and left to -O and double bonds up and right to O. To the left of this is an arrow pointing left to a pyruvate enolate molecule, indicating this is step 6: pyruvate enolate reacts with CO2 to form oxaloacetate. The pyruvate enolate molecule begins with C which bonds up and left to -O, double bonds up and right to O, and bonds down to C. C bonds right to O- (which has a red arrow pointing to the bond line).
